1.problem: Find the sum of all real solutions to \(x^2+\cos x=2019\).
1.solutions: The left-hand side is an even function, hence for each \(x\) that solves the equation, \(-x\) will also be a solution. Pairing the solutions up in this way, we get that the sum must be 0.

2.problem: There are 100 people in a room with ages \(1,2,\ldots,100\). A pair of people is called cute if each of them is at least seven years older than half the age of the other person in the pair. At most how many pairwise disjoint cute pairs can be formed in this room?
2.solutions: For a cute pair \((a,b)\) we would have \[a\ge\frac b2+7,\quad b\ge\frac a2+7.\] Solving the system, we get that \(a\) and \(b\) must both be at least 14. However 14 could only be paired with itself or a smaller number; therefore, only people with age 15 or above can be paired with someone of different age. Pairing consecutive numbers \((15,16),(17,18),\ldots,(99,100)\) works, giving \(\frac{100-14}{2}=43\) pairs.

3.problem: Let \(S(x)\) denote the sum of the digits of a positive integer \(x\). Find the maximum possible value of \(S(x+2019)-S(x)\).
3.solutions: We note that \(S(a+b)\le S(a)+S(b)\) for all positive \(a\) and \(b\), since carrying over will only decrease the sum of digits. (A bit more rigorously, one can show that \(S(x+a\cdot10^b)-S(x)\le a\) for \(0\le a\le9\).) Hence we have \(S(x+2019)-S(x)\le S(2019)=12\), and equality can be achieved with \(x=100000\) for example.

4.problem: Tessa has a figure created by adding a semicircle of radius 1 on each side of an equilateral triangle with side length 2, with semicircles oriented outwards. She then marks two points on the boundary of the figure. What is the greatest possible distance between the two points?
4.solutions: Note that both points must be in different semicircles to reach the maximum distance. Let these points be \(M\) and \(N\), and \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) be the centers of the two semicircles where they lie respectively. Then \[MN\le MO_1+O_1O_2+O_2N.\] Note that the the right side will always be equal to 3 (\(MO_1=O_2N=1\) from the radius condition, and \(O_1O_2=1\) from being a midline of the equliateral triangle), hence \(MN\) can be at most 3. Finally, if the four points are collinear (when \(M\) and \(N\) are defined as the intersection of line \(O_1O_2\) with the two semicircles), then equality will hold. Therefore, the greatest possible distance between \(M\) and \(N\) is 3.

5.problem: Call a positive integer \(n\) weird if \(n\) does not divide \((n-2)!\). Determine the number of weird numbers between 2 and 100 inclusive.
5.solutions:
We claim that all the weird numbers are all the prime numbers and 4. Since no numbers between 1 and \(p-2\) divide prime \(p\), \((p-2)!\) will not be divisible by \(p\). We also have \(2!=2\) not being a multiple of 4.

Now we show that all other numbers are not weird. If \(n=pq\) where \(p\ne q\) and \(p,q\ge2\), then since \(p\) and \(q\) both appear in \(1,2,\ldots,n-2\) and are distinct, we have \(pq\mid(n-2)!\). This leaves the only case of \(n=p^2\) for prime \(p\ge3\). In this case, we can note that \(p\) and \(2p\) are both less than \(p^2-2\), so \(2p^2\mid(n-2)!\) and we are similarly done.

Since there are 25 prime numbers not exceeding 100, there are \(25+1=26\) weird numbers.

6.problem: The pairwise products \(ab,bc,cd\), and \(da\) of positive integers \(a,b,c\), and \(d\) are 64, 88, 120, and 165 in some order. Find \(a+b+c+d\).
6.solutions: The sum \(ab+bc+cd+da=(a+c)(b+d)=437=19\cdot23\), so \(\{a+c,b+d\}=\{19,23\}\) as having either pair sum to 1 is impossible. Then the sum of all 4 is \(19+23=42\). (In fact, it is not difficult to see that the only possible solutions are \((a,b,c,d)=(8,8,11,15)\) or its cyclic permutations and reflections.)

7.problem: For any real number \(\alpha\), define \[\operatorname{sign}(\alpha)=\begin{cases}+1&\text{if }\alpha>0,\\0&\text{if }\alpha=0,\\-1&\text{if }\alpha<0.\end{cases}\] How many triples \((x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\) satisfy the following system of equations \[\begin{aligned} x&=2018-2019\cdot\operatorname{sign}(y+z),\\ y&=2018-2019\cdot\operatorname{sign}(z+x),\\ z&=2018-2019\cdot\operatorname{sign}(x+y)? \end{aligned}\]
7.solutions: Since \(\operatorname{sign}(x+y)\) can take one of 3 values, \(z\) can be one of 3 values: 4037, 2018, or \(-1\). The same is true of \(x\) and \(y\). However, this shows that \(x+y\) cannot be 0, so \(z\) can only be 4037 or \(-1\). The same is true of \(x\) and \(y\). Now note that, if any two of \(x,y,z\) are \(-1\), then the third one must be 4037. Furthermore, if any one of \(x,y,z\) is 4037, then the other two must be \(-1\). Thus, the only possibility is to have exactly two of \(x,y,z\) be \(-1\) and the third one be 4037. This means that the only remaining triples are \((-1,-1,4037)\) and its permutations. These all work, so there are exactly 3 ordered triples.

8.problem: A regular hexagon \(PROFIT\) has area 1. Every minute, greedy George places the largest possible equilateral triangle that does not overlap with other already-placed triangles in the hexagon, with ties broken arbitrarily. How many triangles would George need to cover at least \(90\%\) of the hexagon’s area?
8.solutions:
It’s not difficult to see that the first triangle must connect three non-adjacent vertices (e.g. \(POI\)), which covers area \(\frac12\), and leaves three 30-30-120 triangles of area \(\frac16\) each. Then, the next three triangles cover \(\frac13\) of the respective small triangle they are in, and leave six 30-30-120 triangles of area \(\frac1{18}\) each.

This process continues, doubling the number of 30-30-120 triangles each round and the area of each triangle is divided by 3 each round. After \(1+3+6+12+24=46\) triangles, the remaining area is \(\frac{3\cdot2^4}{6\cdot3^4}=\frac{48}{486}=\frac8{81}<0.1\), and the last triangle removed triangle has area \(\frac1{486}\), so this is the minimum number necessary.

9.problem:
Define \(P=\{S,T\}\) and let \(\mathcal{P}\) be the set of all proper subsets of \(P\). (A proper subset is a subset that is not the set itself.) How many ordered pairs \((\mathcal{S},\mathcal{T})\) of proper subsets of \(\mathcal{P}\) are there such that

(a) \(\mathcal{S}\) is not a proper subset of \(\mathcal{T}\) and \(\mathcal{T}\) is not a proper subset of \(\mathcal{S}\); and

(b) for any sets \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) and \(T\in\mathcal{T}\), \(S\) is not a proper subset of \(T\) and \(T\) is not a proper subset of \(S\)?
9.solutions:
For ease of notation, we let \(0=\varnothing\), \(1=\{S\}\), \(2=\{T\}\). Then both \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\mathcal{T}\) are proper subsets of \(\{0,1,2\}\). We consider the following cases:

Case 1. If \(\mathcal{S}=\varnothing\), then \(\mathcal{S}\) is a proper subset of anyset except the empty set, so we must have \(\mathcal{T}=\varnothing\).

Case 2. If \(\mathcal{S}=\{0\}\), then \(\mathcal{T}\) cannot be empty, nor can it contain either 1 or 2, so we must have \(\mathcal{T}=\{0\}\). This also implies that if \(\mathcal{S}\) contains another element, then there would be no choice of \(\mathcal{T}\) because \(\{0\}\) would be a proper subset.

Case 3. If \(\mathcal{S}=\{1\}\), then \(\mathcal{T}\) cannot contain 0, and cannot contain both 1 and 2 (or it becomes a proper superset of \(\mathcal{S}\)), so it can only be \(\{1\}\) or \(\{2\}\), and both work. The similar apply when \(\mathcal{S}=\{2\}\).

Case 4. If \(\mathcal{S}=\{1,2\}\), then since \(\mathcal{T}\) cannot contain 0, it must contain both 1 and 2 (or it becomes a proper subset of \(\mathcal{S}\)), so \(\mathcal{T}=\{1,2\}\).

Hence, all the possibilities are \[(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{T})=(\varnothing,\varnothing),(\{0\},\{0\}),(\{1\},\{1\}),(\{1\},\{2\}),(\{2\},\{1\}),(\{2\},\{2\}),(\{1,2\},\{1,2\}),\] for 7 possible pairs in total.

10.solutions: Note that \[A=((1+2\sqrt2)(1+3\sqrt3))((2+\sqrt3)(1+3\sqrt2))((3+\sqrt2)(1+2\sqrt3))((3+\sqrt3)(2+\sqrt2)),\] \[B=((1+3\sqrt2)(1+2\sqrt3))((2+\sqrt2)(1+3\sqrt3))((3+\sqrt3)(1+2\sqrt2))((2+\sqrt3)(3+\sqrt2)).\] It is not difficult to check that they have the exact same set of factors, so \(A=B\) and thus the ratio is 1.

11.problem: In the Year 0 of Cambridge there is one squirrel and one rabbit. Both animals multiply in numbers quickly. In particular, if there are \(m\) squirrels and \(n\) rabbits in Year \(k\), then there will be \(2m+2019\) squirrels and \(4n-2\) rabbits in Year \(k+1\). What is the first year in which there will be strictly more rabbits than squirrels?
11.solutions: In year \(k\), the number of squirrels is \[2(2(\cdots(2\cdot1+2019)+2019)+\cdots)+2019=2^k+2019\cdot(2^{k-1}+2^{k-2}+\cdots+1)=2020\cdot2^k-2019\] and the number of rabbits is \[4(4(\cdots(4\cdot1-2)-2)-\cdots)-2=4^k-2\cdot(4^{k-1}+4^{k-2}+\cdots+1)=\frac{4^k+2}{3}.\] For the number of rabbits to exceed that of squirrels, we need \[4^k+2>6060\cdot2^k-6057\iff2^k>6059.\] Since \(2^{13}>6059>2^{12}\), \(k=13\) is the first year for which there are more rabbits than squirrels.

12.problem: Bob is coloring lattice points in the coordinate plane. Find the number of ways Bob can color five points in \(\{(x,y)\mid1\le x,y\le5\}\) blue such that the distance between any two blue points is not an integer.
12.solutions:
We can see that no two blue points can have the same \(x\) or \(y\) coordinate. The blue points then must make a permutation of \(1,2,3,4,5\) that avoid the pattern of 3-4-5 triangles. It is not hard to use complementary counting to get the answer from here.

There are 8 possible pairs of points that are a distance of 5 apart while not being in the same row or column (i.e. a pair that is in the 3-4-5 position). If such a pair of points is included in the choice of five points, then there are \(3!=6\) possibilities for the remaining three points, yielding \(8\times6=48\) configurations that have violations. However, we now need to consider overcounting.

The only way to have more than one violation in one configuration is to have a corner point and then two points adjacent to the opposite corner, e.g. \((1,1),(4,5),(5,4)\). In each such case, there are exactly \(2!=2\) possibilities for the other two points, and there are exactly two violations so there are a total of \(2\times4=8\) configurations that are double-counted.

Therefore, there are \(48-8=40\) permutations that violate the no-integer-condition, leaving \(120-40=80\) good configurations.

13.problem: Reimu has \(2019\) coins \(C_0,C_1,\ldots,C_{2018}\), one of which is fake, though they look identical to each other (so each of them is equally likely to be fake). She has a machine that takes any two coins and picks one that is not fake. If both coins are not fake, the machine picks one uniformly at random. For each \(i=1,2,\ldots,1009\), she puts \(C_0\) and \(C_i\) into the machine once, and machine picks \(C_i\). What is the probability that \(C_0\) is fake?
13.solutions: Let \(E\) denote the event that \(C_0\) is fake, and let \(F\) denote the event that the machine picks \(C_i\) over \(C_0\) for all \(i=1,2,\ldots,1009\). By the definition of conditional probability, \(P(E\mid F)=\frac{P(E\cap F)}{P(F)}\). Since \(E\) implies \(F\), \(P(E\cap F)=P(E)=\frac{1}{2019}\). Now we want to compute \(P(F)\). If \(C_0\) is fake, \(F\) is guaranteed to happen. If \(C_i\) is fake for some \(1\le i\le1009\), then \(F\) is impossible. Finally, if \(C_i\) is fake for some \(1010\le i\le2018\), then \(F\) occurs with probability \(2^{-1009}\), since there is a \(\frac{1}{2}\) probability for each machine decision. Therefore, \[P(F)=\frac{1}{2019}\cdot1+\frac{1009}{2019}\cdot0+\frac{1009}{2019}\cdot2^{-1009}=\frac{2^{1009}+1009}{2019\cdot2^{1009}}.\] Therefore, \(P(E\mid F)=\frac{2^{1009}}{2^{1009}+1009}\).

14.problem: Let \(ABC\) be a triangle where \(AB=9\), \(BC=10\), \(CA=17\). Let \(\Omega\) be its circumcircle, and let \(A_1,B_1,C_1\) be the diametrically opposite points from \(A,B,C\), respectively, on \(\Omega\). Find the area of the convex hexagon with the vertices \(A,B,C,A_1,B_1,C_1\).
14.solutions:
We first compute the circumradius of \(ABC\): Since \(\cos A=\frac{9^2-17^2-10^2}{2\cdot9\cdot17}=-\frac{15}{17}\), we have \(\sin A=\frac{8}{17}\) and \(R=\frac{a}{2\sin A}=\frac{170}{16}\). Moreover, we get that the area of triangle \(ABC\) is \(\frac{1}{2}bc\sin A=36\).

Note that triangle \(ABC\) is obtuse, The area of the hexagon is equal to twice the area of triangle \(ABC\) (which is really \([ABC]+[A_1B_1C_1]\)) plus the area of rectangle \(ACA_1C_1\). The dimensions of \(ACA_1C_1\) are \(AC=17\) and \(A_1C=\sqrt{(2R)^2-AC^2}=\frac{51}{4}\), so the area of the hexagon is \(36\cdot2+17\cdot\frac{51}{4}=\frac{1155}{4}\).

15.problem:
Five people are at a party. Each pair of them are friends, enemies, or frenemies (which is equivalent to being both friends and enemies). It is known that given any three people \(A,B,C\):

  • If \(A\) and \(B\) are friends and \(B\) and \(C\) are friends, then \(A\) and \(C\) are friends;
  • If \(A\) and \(B\) are enemies and \(B\) and \(C\) are enemies, then \(A\) and \(C\) are friends;
  • If \(A\) and \(B\) are friends and \(B\) and \(C\) are enemies, then \(A\) and \(C\) are enemies.

How many possible relationship configurations are there among the five people?
15.solutions:
If \(A\) and \(B\) are frenemies, then regardless of whether another person \(C\) is friends or enemies with \(A\), \(C\) will have to be frenemies with \(B\) and vice versa. Therefore, if there is one pair of frenemies then all of them are frenemies with each other, and there is only one possibility.

If there are no frenemies, then one can always separate the five people into two possibly “factions” (one of which may be empty) such that two people are friends if and only if they belong to the same faction. Since the factions are unordered, there are \(2^5/2=16\) ways to assign the “alignments” that each gives a unique configuration of relations. So in total there are \(16+1=17\) possibilities.

16.problem:
Let \(\mathbb{R}\) be the set of real numbers. Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be a function such that for all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), we have \[f(x^2)+f(y^2)=f(x+y)^2-2xy.\]

Let \(S=\sum_{n=-2019}^{2019}f(n)\). Determine the number of possible values of \(S\).
16.solutions:
Letting \(y=-x\) gives \[f(x^2)+f(x^2)=f(0)^2+2x^2\] for all \(x\). When \(x=0\) the equation above gives \(f(0)=0\) or \(f(0)=2\).

If \(f(0)=2\), then \(f(x)=x+2\) for all nonnegative \(x\), so the LHS becomes \(x^2+y^2+4\), and RHS becomes \(x^2+y^2+4x+4y+4\) for all \(x+y\ge0\), which cannot be equal to LHS if \(x+y>0\).

If \(f(0)=0\) then \(f(x)=x\) for all nonnegative \(x\). Moreover, letting \(y=0\) gives \[f(x^2)=f(x)^2\implies f(x)=\pm x\] for all \(x\). Since negative values are never used as inputs on the LHS and the output on the RHS is always squared, we may conclude that for all negative \(x\), \(f(x)=x\) and \(f(x)=-x\) are both possible (and the values are independent). Therefore, the value of \(S\) can be written as \[S=f(0)+(f(1)+f(-1))+(f(2)+f(-2))+\cdots+(f(2019)+f(-2019))=2\sum_{i=1}^{2019}i\delta_i\] for \(\delta_1,\delta_2,\ldots,\delta_{2019}\in\{0,1\}\). It is not difficult to see that \(\frac{S}{2}\) can take any integer value between \(0\) and \(\frac{2020\cdot2019}{2}=2039190\) inclusive, so there are \(2039191\) possible values of \(S\).

17.problem: Let \(ABC\) be a triangle with \(AB=3\), \(BC=4\), and \(CA=5\). Let \(A_1,A_2\) be points on side \(BC\), \(B_1,B_2\) be points on side \(CA\), and \(C_1,C_2\) be points on side \(AB\). Suppose that there exists a point \(P\) such that \(PA_1A_2\), \(PB_1B_2\), and \(PC_1C_2\) are congruent equilateral triangles. Find the area of convex hexagon \(A_1A_2B_1B_2C_1C_2\).
17.solutions:
Since \(P\) is the shared vertex between the three equilateral triangles, \(P\) is the incenter of \(ABC\), because it is equidistant from all three sides. The area and semiperimeter of \(ABC\) are both \(6\), so the inradius is \(1\). Thus each equilateral triangle has altitude \(1\), and hence side length \(2/\sqrt{3}\).

It follows that \[AB_2=AC_1=2-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}},\qquad BA_1=BC_2=1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}},\qquad CB_1=CA_2=3-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\] Subtracting the three corner triangles from \(ABC\), the desired area is \[6-\left[ \frac12\left(2-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2\frac45 +\frac12\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2 +\frac12\left(3-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2\frac35 \right] =\boxed{\frac{12+22\sqrt3}{15}}.\]

18.problem: 2019 points are chosen independently and uniformly at random on the interval \([0,1]\). Tairitsu picks 1000 of them randomly and colors them black, leaving the remaining ones white. Hikari then computes the sum of the positions of the leftmost white point and the rightmost black point. What is the probability that this sum is at most \(1\)?
18.solutions: Reflect every black point across \(1/2\), sending its position \(x\) to \(1-x\). The reflected black points are still independent and uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\). The given condition is now equivalent to the leftmost point among all \(2019\) points being white. Every point is equally likely to be leftmost, so the desired probability is \[\boxed{\frac{1019}{2019}}.\]

19.problem: Complex numbers \(a,b,c\) form an equilateral triangle with side length \(18\) in the complex plane. If \(|a+b+c|=36\), find \(|bc+ca+ab|\).
19.solutions: Let \(d=(a+b+c)/3\), the center of the equilateral triangle. Then \(|d|=12\). Define \[a'=a-d,\qquad b'=b-d,\qquad c'=c-d.\] Since \(a',b',c'\) are the vertices of an equilateral triangle centered at the origin, \(a'+b'+c'=0\) and \(b'c'+c'a'+a'b'=0\). Therefore \[bc+ca+ab =(b'+d)(c'+d)+(c'+d)(a'+d)+(a'+d)(b'+d) =3d^2.\] Hence \[|bc+ca+ab|=3|d|^2=3\cdot 12^2=\boxed{432}.\]

20.problem: On floor \(0\) of a weird-looking building, you enter an elevator that only has one button. You press the button twice and end up on floor \(1\). Thereafter, every time you press the button, you go up by one floor with probability \(\frac{X}{Y}\), where \(X\) is your current floor, and \(Y\) is the total number of times you have pressed the button thus far (not including the current one); otherwise, the elevator does nothing. Between the third and the 100th press inclusive, what is the expected number of pairs of consecutive presses that both take you up a floor?
20.solutions:
After \(n\) button presses, the elevator is uniformly distributed among floors \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\). This follows by induction from the transition probabilities.

Thus, for \(n\ge 2\), the probability that presses \(n+1\) and \(n+2\) both move the elevator up is \[\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{i}{n}\cdot\frac{i+1}{n+1} =\frac13.\] There are \(97\) pairs of consecutive presses from the third through the hundredth presses, so the expected number is \[97\cdot\frac13=\boxed{\frac{97}{3}}.\]

21.problem: A regular hexagon \(ABCDEF\) has side length \(1\) and center \(O\). Parabolas \(P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_6\) are constructed with common focus \(O\) and directrices \(AB,BC,CD,DE,EF,FA\), respectively. Let \(\chi\) be the set of all distinct points on the plane that lie on at least two of the six parabolas. Compute \[\sum_{X\in\chi}|OX|.\] (Recall that the focus is the point and the directrix is the line such that the parabola is the locus of points that are equidistant from the focus and the directrix.)
21.solutions:
Label the parabolas \(P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_6\) in cyclic order according to their directrices. By rotational symmetry, there are three types of pairs to consider.

For two parabolas with adjacent directrices, such as \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), their two intersection points have distances \[2\sqrt3-3\qquad\text{and}\qquad 2\sqrt3+3\] from \(O\). For two parabolas whose directrices are separated by one side, such as \(P_1\) and \(P_3\), the distances are \[\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\qquad\text{and}\qquad \sqrt3.\] Finally, two parabolas with opposite directrices, such as \(P_1\) and \(P_4\), have two intersection points, each at distance \(\sqrt3/2\) from \(O\).

Accounting for all rotations, the desired sum is \[6(2\sqrt3-3)+6(2\sqrt3+3)+6\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\right) +6\sqrt3+6\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) =\boxed{35\sqrt3}.\]

22.problem:
Determine the number of subsets \(S\) of \(\{1,2,\ldots,1000\}\) that satisfy the following conditions:

  • \(S\) has \(19\) elements, and
  • the sum of the elements in any non-empty subset of \(S\) is not divisible by \(20\).
22.solutions:
Choose any ordering \(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{19}\) of the elements of \(S\). The \(20\) partial sums \[0,a_1,a_1+a_2,\ldots,a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_{19}\] must be distinct modulo \(20\), since equality between two of them would give a nonempty subset whose sum is divisible by \(20\). Thus these partial sums represent every residue class modulo \(20\).

Now interchange any two adjacent elements \(a_i\) and \(a_{i+1}\). Only one of the partial sums changes, but the resulting partial sums must again represent every residue class. Therefore the changed partial sum must remain the same modulo \(20\), so \(a_i\equiv a_{i+1}\pmod{20}\). Hence all elements of \(S\) have the same residue modulo \(20\).

That common residue must be relatively prime to \(20\); conversely, any \(19\) numbers with the same residue relatively prime to \(20\) satisfy the condition. There are \(\varphi(20)=8\) possible residues and \(50\) numbers in each residue class, so the answer is \[\boxed{8\binom{50}{19}}.\]

23.problem: Find the smallest positive integer \(n\) such that \[\underbrace{2^{2^{\cdot^{\cdot^{2}}}}}_{n\text{ 2's}} > \underbrace{(\cdots((100!)!)!\cdots)!}_{100\text{ factorials}}.\]
23.solutions:
Let \(T_m\) denote a tower of \(m\) twos, and let \(F_k\) denote the result of applying \(k\) factorials to \(100\). Note that \(T_4>100^2\).

We claim that \(a>b^2\) implies \(2^a>(b!)^2\) for the values \(b\) that arise here. Indeed, \(2^a>b^{2b}\) is equivalent to \(a>2b\log_2 b\), and \(\log_2 b<b/2\) for \(b>4\). Since \(b^b>b!\), this bound works. It follows by induction that \[T_m>F_{m-4}^2\] for all \(m\ge4\). Thus \(T_{104}>F_{100}\), so \(n=104\) works.

The lower bound follows from the fact that \(m!>2^m\) for \(m>3\). Since \(100>T_3\), repeated application gives \(F_{100}>T_{103}\). Therefore a tower of \(103\) twos is still too small, and the answer is \(\boxed{104}\).

24.problem: Let \(S\) be the set of all positive factors of \(6000\). What is the probability a random quadruple \((a,b,c,d)\in S^4\) satisfies \[\operatorname{lcm}(\gcd(a,b),\gcd(c,d))=\gcd(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b),\operatorname{lcm}(c,d))?\]
24.solutions:
Fix a prime whose exponent in \(6000\) is \(n\), and let its exponents in \(a,b,c,d\) be \(p,q,r,s\), respectively. The required equality holds for this prime exactly when the two middle values among \(p,q,r,s\) are equal.

There are \(n+1\) quadruples in which all four exponents are equal. If exactly two exponent values occur, one must occur three times, giving \[8\binom{n+1}{2}\] quadruples. If exactly three exponent values occur, the middle value must occur twice, giving \[12\binom{n+1}{3}\] quadruples. Thus the probability for this prime is \[\frac{12\binom{n+1}{3}+8\binom{n+1}{2}+(n+1)}{(n+1)^4} =\frac{2n(n+1)+1}{(n+1)^3}.\]

Since \(6000=2^4\cdot3\cdot5^3\), the choices of exponents for the three primes are independent. Therefore the desired probability is \[\frac{41}{125}\cdot\frac58\cdot\frac{25}{64} =\boxed{\frac{41}{512}}.\]

25.problem: A \(5\times 5\) grid of unit squares is partitioned into 5 pairwise incongruent rectangles with sides lying on gridlines. Find the maximum possible product of the areas of the 5 rectangles.
25.solutions:
The maximum is achieved by rectangles of dimensions \(3\times 1\), \(1\times 4\), \(2\times 2\), \(2\times 3\), and \(4\times 2\), where the first dimension is horizontal and the bottom-left corners are, respectively, \[(2,4),\ (4,0),\ (2,2),\ (0,2),\ (0,0).\] The product of their areas is \[3\cdot 4\cdot 4\cdot 6\cdot 8=2304.\]

We now prove that this is maximal. If one rectangle has area at most \(2\), then by AM-GM the product is at most \[2\cdot 5.75^4=2\cdot 33.0625^2<2\cdot 1100=2200.\] If one rectangle has area at least \(9\), then the product is at most \[9\cdot 4^4=2304.\] Neither of these bounds can be attained by five pairwise incongruent rectangles. Thus, in an optimal partition, every rectangle has area between \(3\) and \(8\), inclusive.

There can be at most one rectangle of each of areas \(3,5,6,8\), at most two rectangles of area \(4\), and no rectangle of area \(7\). The only possible multiset of five such areas with sum \(25\) is \[3,4,4,6,8.\] Hence the maximum product is \[\boxed{2304}.\]

26.problem: Let \(ABC\) be a triangle with \(AB=13\), \(BC=14\), \(CA=15\). Let \(I_A,I_B,I_C\) be the \(A,B,C\) excenters of this triangle, and let \(O\) be the circumcenter of the triangle. Let \(\gamma_A,\gamma_B,\gamma_C\) be the corresponding excircles and \(\omega\) be the circumcircle. \(X\) is one of the intersections between \(\gamma_A\) and \(\omega\). Likewise, \(Y\) is an intersection of \(\gamma_B\) and \(\omega\), and \(Z\) is an intersection of \(\gamma_C\) and \(\omega\). Compute \[\cos\angle OXI_A+\cos\angle OYI_B+\cos\angle OZI_C.\]
26.solutions:
Let \(r_A,r_B,r_C\) be the exradii and \(R\) the circumradius. By Euler’s formula, \[OI_A=\sqrt{R(R+2r_A)}.\] The Law of Cosines in triangle \(OXI_A\) gives \[\cos\angle OXI_A =\frac{R^2+r_A^2-R(R+2r_A)}{2Rr_A} =\frac{r_A}{2R}-1.\] The analogous formulas hold for \(I_B\) and \(I_C\), so the desired expression is \[\frac{r_A+r_B+r_C}{2R}-3.\]

Let \(r\) and \(K\) be the inradius and area of \(ABC\). We have \[\begin{aligned} r_A+r_B+r_C-r &=2K\left(\frac1{-a+b+c}+\frac1{a-b+c}+\frac1{a+b-c}-\frac1{a+b+c}\right)\\ &=2K\cdot\frac{8abc}{(4K)^2} =\frac{abc}{K} =4R. \end{aligned}\] Therefore the desired expression is \[\frac{r+4R}{2R}-3=\frac{r}{2R}-1.\] For the \(13\)-\(14\)-\(15\) triangle, \(r=4\) and \(R=\frac{65}{8}\). Hence the answer is \[\frac{4}{65/4}-1=\boxed{-\frac{49}{65}}.\]

27.problem: The eighth-sphere \[\left\{(x,y,z)\mid x,y,z\ge 0,\ x^2+y^2+z^2=1\right\}\] is projected orthogonally onto the plane \(x+y+z=1\). What is the area of the projection?
27.solutions:
Consider the three flat faces of the eighth-ball bounded by the eighth-sphere. Each is a quarter-circle of area \(\frac\pi4\), and their projections onto the plane \(x+y+z=1\) cover the desired region.

The area scale factor for projecting the plane \(x=0\) onto \(x+y+z=1\) is the cosine of the angle between their normal vectors. Thus it is \[\frac{(1,0,0)\cdot(1,1,1)}{\lVert(1,0,0)\rVert\lVert(1,1,1)\rVert} =\frac1{\sqrt3}.\] The same factor applies to the other two coordinate planes. Therefore the area of the projection is \[3\cdot\frac\pi4\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3} =\boxed{\frac{\pi\sqrt3}{4}}.\]

28.problem: How many integers \(a\) with \(2\le a\le 101\) have the following property: there exists a positive integer \(N\) such that the last two digits of the decimal representation of \(a^{2^n}\) are the same for all \(n\ge N\)?
28.solutions:
Solution 1. The fixed points of squaring modulo \(100\) are \(0,1,25,76\). We solve backward from each of these residues.

The residues that eventually reach \(0\) or \(25\) are exactly the multiples of \(5\), giving \(20\) possibilities. The square roots of \(1\) modulo \(100\) are \[1,49,51,99,\] and the new square roots obtained from \(49\) are \[7,43,57,93.\] Similarly, the square roots of \(76\) are \[24,26,74,76,\] and the new square roots obtained from \(24\) are \[18,32,68,82.\] These give \(16\) possibilities not divisible by \(5\). Thus the answer is \[20+16=\boxed{36}.\]

Solution 2. We seek the elements of \(\mathbb Z_{100}\) whose repeated squaring eventually reaches a fixed point. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, we may work independently modulo \(4\) and modulo \(25\).

All \(4\) residues modulo \(4\) work. Modulo \(25\), all \(5\) multiples of \(5\) work. The remaining \(20\) residues form the multiplicative group modulo \(25\), which is cyclic of order \(20\). After choosing a primitive root, repeated squaring corresponds to the map \[y\longmapsto 2y\] on \(\mathbb Z_{20}\). The residues that eventually reach the fixed point \(0\) are the \(4\) multiples of \(5\). Thus \(5+4=9\) residues modulo \(25\) work, and the total number modulo \(100\) is \[4\cdot 9=\boxed{36}.\]

29.problem: A positive integer \(N\) is chosen at random such that \[\Pr(N=n)=\frac1{2^n}\] for every positive integer \(n\). A hat contains \(N\) slips of paper numbered \(1,2,\ldots,N\). Annie draws one slip uniformly at random and sees that it is numbered \(2\). What is the expected value of \(N\)?
29.solutions:
Let \(S\) be the number on the slip drawn, and set \[X=\Pr(S=2)=\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{2^{-k}}{k}.\] By Bayes’ theorem, \[\Pr(N=n\mid S=2)= \begin{cases} \frac{2^{-n}/n}{X},&n\ge2,\\ 0,&n=1. \end{cases}\] Therefore \[\mathbb E[N\mid S=2] =\frac1X\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}2^{-n} =\frac1{2X}.\]

Integrating the geometric series gives \[\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{x^k}{k}=-\ln(1-x).\] At \(x=\frac12\), this yields \[X=\ln2-\frac12.\] Hence \[\mathbb E[N\mid S=2] =\frac1{2\ln2-1} =\boxed{\frac1{2\ln2-1}}.\]

30.problem: Three points are chosen uniformly and independently at random from the interior of a unit cube. What is the probability that there exists a cube of side length \(\frac12\), with edges parallel to those of the unit cube, that contains all three points?
30.solutions:
Project the three points onto each of the three coordinate axes. The points fit in a cube of side length \(\frac12\) exactly when, on each axis, the three projections fit in an interval of length \(\frac12\). These three events are independent.

For one axis, order the projected points as \(p<q<r\), and let \[a=p,\qquad b=q-p,\qquad c=r-q,\qquad d=1-r.\] The spacings \((a,b,c,d)\) are uniformly distributed on the simplex \(a+b+c+d=1\). The three points fit in an interval of length \(\frac12\) exactly when \[r-q\le\frac12,\] or \(b+c\le\frac12\). By symmetry between \(a+d\) and \(b+c\), this has probability \(\frac12\).

Consequently, the desired probability is \[\left(\frac12\right)^3=\boxed{\frac18}.\]

31.problem: In triangle \(ABC\), \(AB=6\), \(AC=7\), and \(BC=8\), and \(I\) is the incenter. Points \(Z\) and \(Y\) lie in the interiors of \(AB\) and \(AC\), respectively, such that \(YZ\) is tangent to the incircle. Let \(P\) be a point such that \[\angle ZPC=\angle YPB=90^\circ.\] Find \(IP\).
31.solutions:
Solution 1. Let \(PU\) and \(PV\) be the two tangents from \(P\) to the incircle. We invoke the dual of the Desargues Involution Theorem. Given a point \(P\) and four lines \(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\), the set of conics tangent to all four lines determines an involution on the lines through \(P\): a tangent to one of these conics is paired with the other tangent from \(P\). If \(A,B,C,D,E,F\) are the vertices of the complete quadrilateral formed by the four lines, then the involution pairs \(PA\) with \(PD\), \(PB\) with \(PE\), and \(PC\) with \(PF\). References for this theorem include \[\texttt{https://www.scribd.com/document/384321704/Desargues-Involution-Theorem}\] and \[\texttt{https://www2.washjeff.edu/users/mwoltermann/Dorrie/63.pdf}.\]

Apply this theorem to \(P\) and the four lines \(AB,AC,BC,YZ\). The three pairs of lines swapped by the involution are \[(PU,PV),\qquad(PY,PB),\qquad(PZ,PC).\] The last two pairs are each perpendicular, so this involution on the pencil of lines through \(P\) is rotation by \(90^\circ\). It follows that \(PU\perp PV\), so \(IUPV\) is a square. Therefore \[IP=r\sqrt2.\] By Heron’s formula, the area of \(ABC\) is \(\frac{21\sqrt{15}}4\), so \[r=\frac{2K}{a+b+c} =\frac{21\sqrt{15}/2}{21} =\frac{\sqrt{15}}2.\] Thus \[IP=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{30}}2}.\]

Solution 2. Let \(H\) be the orthocenter. We use the identity \[HI^2=2r^2-4R^2\cos A\cos B\cos C.\] This follows, for example, by applying the barycentric identity \[aXA^2+bXB^2+cXC^2 =(a+b+c)XI^2+aAI^2+bBI^2+cCI^2\] and then simplifying trigonometrically.

Let \(E=BH\cap AC\) and \(F=CH\cap AB\). The points \(B,P,E,Y\) lie on a circle with diameter \(BY\), and \(C,P,F,Z\) lie on a circle with diameter \(CZ\). Let \(Q\) be the second intersection of these two circles. Since \(BCYZ\) is a tangential quadrilateral, the midpoints of \(BY\) and \(CZ\) are collinear with \(I\) by Newton’s theorem. It follows by symmetry that \[IP=IQ.\]

Also, \[BH\cdot HE=CH\cdot HF,\] so \(H\) lies on the radical axis \(PQ\) of the two circles. If \(IP=IQ=x\), then \[BH\cdot HE=x^2-HI^2.\] The claim \(x=r\sqrt2\) is therefore equivalent to \[BH\cdot HE=4R^2\cos A\cos B\cos C.\] But \[BH\cdot HE=BH\cdot CH\cos A =(2R\cos B)(2R\cos C)\cos A,\] which proves the claim. Hence \(IP=r\sqrt2=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{30}}2}\).

Note. There is also a shorter method under the assumption that the problem is well-posed. Let \(U\) be a point of tangency on the incircle such that \(IU\parallel BC\), and choose \(YZ\perp BC\) tangent to the incircle at \(U\). Taking the appropriate intersection point \(P\), one obtains a square \(IUPD\), where \(D\) is the corresponding point of tangency, and hence \(IP=r\sqrt2\). This argument disregards the condition that \(Y\) and \(Z\) lie in the interiors of the sides, but the condition is indeed satisfied in this configuration.

32.problem: For positive integers \(a\) and \(b\) such that \(a\) is coprime to \(b\), define \(\operatorname{ord}_b(a)\) as the least positive integer \(k\) such that \(b\mid a^k-1\), and define \(\phi(a)\) to be the number of positive integers less than or equal to \(a\) which are coprime to \(a\). Find the least positive integer \(n\) such that \[\operatorname{ord}_n(m)<\frac{\phi(n)}{10}\] for all positive integers \(m\) coprime to \(n\).
32.solutions:
The maximum order of an element modulo \(n\) is the Carmichael function, denoted \(\lambda(n)\). The following properties of the Carmichael function are established:

  • For primes \(p>2\) and positive integers \(k\), \[\lambda(p^k)=(p-1)p^{k-1}.\]
  • For a positive integer \(k\), \[\lambda(2^k)= \begin{cases} 2^{k-2},&k\ge3,\\ 2^{k-1},&k\le2. \end{cases}\]
  • For a positive integer \(n\) with prime factorization \(n=\prod p_i^{k_i}\), \[\lambda(n)=\operatorname{lcm}\left(\lambda(p_1^{k_1}),\lambda(p_2^{k_2}),\ldots\right).\]

Meanwhile, for \(n=\prod p_i^{k_i}\), we have \[\phi(n)=\prod(p_i-1)p_i^{k_i-1}.\] Hence the intuition is roughly that the \((p_i-1)p_i^{k_i-1}\) terms must share divisors in order to reach a high value of \(\frac{\phi(n)}{\lambda(n)}\).

We will now show that \(n\ge240\) by doing casework on the prime divisors of \[z=\frac{\phi(n)}{\lambda(n)}.\] Suppose \(p\mid z\) and \(p>2\). This requires two terms among \[\lambda(p_1^{k_1}),\lambda(p_2^{k_2}),\ldots\] to be multiples of \(p\), because \(\lambda(n)\) is the least common multiple of the terms whereas the product of these numbers has the same number of factors of \(p\) as \(\phi(n)\). Note that this does not hold for \(p=2\), because \(\lambda(2^k)\ne2^{k-1}\) in general. These multiples correspond to either \(p^2\mid n\) or \(q\mid n\) with \(q\equiv1\pmod p\). Therefore \[n\ge\max\left(p^2(2p+1),(2p+1)(4p+1)\right),\] because the smallest primes congruent to \(1\pmod p\) are at least \(2p+1\) and \(4p+1\). For \(p\ge5\), this gives \(n>240\), so we may assume \(p\le3\).

First we address the case \(p=3\). This means that two numbers among \[9,7,13,19,31,37,\ldots\] divide \(n\). As \(7\cdot37>240\), we discard primes greater than \(31\). Of the remaining numbers, we have \[\lambda(9)=6,\quad \lambda(7)=6,\quad \lambda(13)=12,\quad \lambda(19)=18,\quad \lambda(31)=30.\] No candidate value of \(n\) is the product of just two of these numbers, as the greatest common divisor of any two of the associated \(\lambda\)-values is at most \(6\). Furthermore, multiplying by just \(2\) will not affect \(\phi(n)\) or \(\lambda(n)\), so we must multiply at least two of these numbers by a number greater than \(2\). Throwing out numbers greater than \(240\), this leaves only \(3\cdot9\cdot7\), which does not work. A close candidate is \(3\cdot7\cdot13=273\), for which \(\phi(n)=144\) and \(\lambda(n)=12\).

The remaining case is when the only prime divisors of \(\frac{\phi(n)}{\lambda(n)}\) are \(2\). It is not hard to see that \(\lambda(n)\ge4\) when \(n\nmid24\); when \(n\mid24\), it is clear that \(\phi(n)\le8\), so we need not consider those values. When \(\lambda(n)=4\), we need \[\phi(n)\ge4\cdot2^4=64\] and \(v_2(n)\le4\), so the smallest such integer is \[n=2^4\cdot3\cdot5=240,\] which we can check indeed satisfies \(\frac{\phi(n)}{\lambda(n)}>10\). It is not difficult to check that higher values of \(\lambda(n)\) yield no \(n<240\). Therefore the least possible value is \[\boxed{240}.\]

Note. The sequence \(\frac{\phi(n)}{\lambda(n)}\) is A034380 in the OEIS.
